help.excerpt: Vasilissa the Wise opened her window and asked: "What are you crying for, Prince?" "How can I help crying? Your father has ordered me to plant a garden in one night!" "That's nothing! lie down and sleep: the morning is wiser than the evening." She made him go to sleep, but she herself went out on the steps, called and whistled with a mighty whistle. From every side there ran together gardeners of all sorts, and they planted a garden green, and in the garden birds sang, on the trees flowers blossomed, from the boughs hung ripe apples and pears. Early in the morning Vasilissa the Wise awoke the Prince: "Get up, Prince! the garden is ready: Papa is coming to see it."

narrativeBlocks.title: A favor becomes a debt
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ralston's tale, an eagle first asks the king to spare it and feed it. Years later, it carries him across the sea, where a promise leads the king's son into the Water King's service.

narrativeBlocks.title: The first task
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Ralston's English text; whitespace normalized): “The Water King saw him, and said: "Hail, friend! why have you been so long in coming to me? I have grown weary of waiting for you. Now set to work. Here is your first task. Build me in one night a great crystal bridge, so that it shall be ready for use to-morrow.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Vasilissa answers the problem
narrativeBlocks.body: The prince despairs over the deadline. Vasilissa tells him to sleep, summons builders with a whistle, and the bridge is ready by morning.

narrativeBlocks.title: A collected folktale, not a universal myth
narrativeBlocks.body: Ralston records a Russian folk tale with motifs that also occur elsewhere. The specific eagle, task, and Vasilissa episode belong to this version.

narrativeBlocks.title: Bargains have consequences
narrativeBlocks.body: The tale connects a saved animal, a favor repaid, and an impossible task imposed on the king's son.
